To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a generic product of the combination antibiotic piperacillin–tazobactam, characterized by pharmaceutical and kinetic equivalence but a faulty sigmoid fit of Hill’s pharmacodynamic model, promoted bacterial resistance to piperacillin in an animal model.
the pharmacodynamic nonequivalent behavior of a generic piperacillin–tazobactam formulation, as compared with the innovators, promoted the emergence of resistant bacteria in vivo.

the generic product of p-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) that we studied was not pharmacodynamically equivalent to the innovator, and this nonequivalence resulted in a 20-fold increase in the resistant subpopulation after only 24 hours.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact on the resistance of bacteria of the pharmacodynamic nonequivalencies of generic antibiotics, and it is a continuation of our previous research on the same topic.
the development of new strategies to prevent bacterial resistance, which is one of the major public health problems of our time.
the impact on the emergence of bacterial resistance of the therapeutic nonequivalence that may be present in generic antibiotics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in general, pharmaceutical equivalence, pharmacokinetic equivalence, and pharmacodynamic equivalence should be considered as necessary and sufficient conditions for therapeutic equivalence of generic drugs.
the generic piperacillin–tazobactam product tested here is therapeutically nonequivalent to the innovator.
pharmaceutical equivalence and/or pharmacokinetic equivalence are not sufficient conditions for therapeutic equivalence of generic antibiotics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the therapeutic nonequivalence (pharmacodynamic nonequivalence) of generic antibiotics could be a major factor contributing to the problem of resistance.
“generic is generic” is no more a sufficient condition for therapeutic equivalence.
“the more similar the generic is to the innovator, the more similar the impact in vivo is on bacterial resistance”.
The main takeaway from our work is that

pharmaceutical and pharmacokinetics equivalence is a necessary but not sufficient condition to guarantee therapeutic equivalence of generic antibiotics, and that even subtle deviations from therapeutic equivalence could have a significant negative impact on bacterial resistance.
even subtle differences in pharmacodynamic profiles of generic antibiotics can have a major impact on the emergence of resistance in the target bacterial population.
even subtle deviations from therapeutic equivalence can be sufficient to promote resistance in the clinic.
